claim: The human genome encodes over 150 lipid transfer proteins (LTPs).
source: The human genome encodes over 150 LTPs; new LTPs and LTP families are being characterized every so often (Wong et al., 2019; Gatta et al., 2015; Sandhu et al., 2018; Valverde et al., 2019; Osawa et al., 2019; Yeo et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2018; Castro et al., 2022; Neuman et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2019 and other references

claim: About 50 LTPs are secreted and involved in carrying lipids, metals, lipopolysaccharides, and other small molecules in blood plasma.
source: About 50 of these proteins are secreted and are involved in carrying lipids, metals, lipopolysaccharides, and other small molecules in blood plasma (Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2019

claim: The remaining intracellular LTPs are mainly responsible for intracellular lipid trafficking among organelles.
source: The remaining intracellular LTPs are mainly responsible for intracellular lipid trafficking among organelles.
evidence: Based on established understanding of LTP function

claim: LTP-mediated trafficking of ceramide from the ER to the trans-Golgi is needed for sphingomyelin synthesis.
source: For example, LTP-mediated trafficking of ceramide from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the trans-Golgi is needed for sphingomyelin synthesis (Hanada et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanada et al., 2003

claim: An arrayed gene knockout library targeting 90 intracellular LTPs was created based on CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
source: To study LTPs systematically, we designed and created an arrayed gene knockout library targeting 90 intracellular LTPs based on the CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
evidence: Describes the experimental approach taken in this study

claim: In the library, 90 wells of a 96-well plate were used for targeting LTPs and 6 for non-targeting controls.
source: In this library, 90 wells of a 96-well plate were used for targeting LTPs and 6 for non-targeting (NT) controls (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes the library design and references Figure 1A

claim: Three guide RNAs per gene were used for optimal gene disruption.
source: For optimal gene disruption, we used a lentiviral gene delivery system and three guide RNAs per gene – a method also used by others to increase the frequency of gene disruption (Wong et al., 2023).
evidence: Describes the methodology and cites Wong et al., 2023

claim: The LTP knockout library was applied to MelJuSo, a human melanoma cell line.
source: We applied the LTP knockout library to MelJuSo, a human melanoma cell line.
evidence: Describes the experimental system used

claim: The efficiency of the knockout strategy was confirmed by western blotting of selected wells.
source: The efficiency of the knockout strategy was confirmed by western blotting of selected wells (Figure 1B).
evidence: References Figure 1B showing western blot validation

claim: Lipidomics analysis of the LTP knockout cells confirmed known lipid disturbances.
source: Lipidomics analysis of the library-generated LTP knockout cells confirmed known and identified novel lipid disturbances emerging from loss of LTPs.
evidence: Describes results from lipidomics analysis

claim: Lipidomics analysis of the LTP knockout cells identified novel lipid disturbances.
source: Lipidomics analysis of the library-generated LTP knockout cells confirmed known and identified novel lipid disturbances emerging from loss of LTPs.
evidence: Describes results from lipidomics analysis

claim: CERT, GLTP, NPC1, and NPC2 knockout cells showed altered sphingolipid levels.
source: These included CERT, GLTP, NPC1, and NPC2 knockout cells with altered sphingolipid levels.
evidence: Describes results from lipidomics analysis

claim: Major sphingolipid imbalances were identified in ORP9 and ORP11 knockout cells.
source: Furthermore, we identified major sphingolipid imbalances in ORP9 and ORP11 knockout cells, two proteins of unknown function in sphingolipid metabolism.
evidence: Describes results from lipidomics analysis

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 were previously of unknown function in sphingolipid metabolism.
source: Furthermore, we identified major sphingolipid imbalances in ORP9 and ORP11 knockout cells, two proteins of unknown function in sphingolipid metabolism.
evidence: States the prior knowledge status of these proteins

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 form a heterodimer.
source: ORP9 and ORP11 form a heterodimer to localize at the ER-trans-Golgi membrane contact sites, where the dimer exchanges phosphatidylserine (PS) for phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI(4)P) between the two organelles.
evidence: Describes findings from this study

claim: The ORP9-ORP11 heterodimer localizes at the ER-trans-Golgi membrane contact sites.
source: ORP9 and ORP11 form a heterodimer to localize at the ER-trans-Golgi membrane contact sites, where the dimer exchanges phosphatidylserine (PS) for phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI(4)P) between the two organelles.
evidence: Describes findings from this study

claim: The ORP9-ORP11 dimer exchanges phosphatidylserine (PS) for phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI(4)P) between the ER and trans-Golgi.
source: ORP9 and ORP11 form a heterodimer to localize at the ER-trans-Golgi membrane contact sites, where the dimer exchanges phosphatidylserine (PS) for phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI(4)P) between the two organelles.
evidence: Describes findings from this study

claim: Loss of either ORP9 or ORP11 causes phospholipid imbalances in the Golgi apparatus.
source: Consequently, loss of either protein causes phospholipid imbalances in the Golgi apparatus that result in lowered sphingomyelin synthesis at this organelle.
evidence: Describes findings from this study

claim: Loss of either ORP9 or ORP11 results in lowered sphingomyelin synthesis at the Golgi apparatus.
source: Consequently, loss of either protein causes phospholipid imbalances in the Golgi apparatus that result in lowered sphingomyelin synthesis at this organelle.
evidence: Describes findings from this study

claim: Many lipids are heterogeneously distributed among organelles.
source: Many types of lipids are heterogeneously distributed among various organelles of the cell (van Meer and de Kroon, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Meer and de Kroon, 2011

claim: Vesicular trafficking transports lipids in bulk between organelles.
source: While vesicular trafficking transports lipids in bulk between organelles, non-vesicular trafficking of lipids also plays a role in defining the lipid compositions of organelles.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lipid trafficking

claim: Non-vesicular trafficking of lipids plays a role in defining the lipid compositions of organelles.
source: While vesicular trafficking transports lipids in bulk between organelles, non-vesicular trafficking of lipids also plays a role in defining the lipid compositions of organelles.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lipid trafficking

claim: Many organelles that do not receive any vesicular cargo rely on non-vesicular lipid trafficking.
source: In fact, many organelles that do not receive any vesicular cargo rely on this route.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lipid trafficking

claim: Non-vesicular trafficking of lipids is achieved by LTPs that carry lipids using their hydrophobic cavities.
source: Non-vesicular trafficking of lipids is achieved by a group of LTPs that carry lipids using their hydrophobic cavities to stabilize lipids in the aqueous intracellular environment (Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2019

claim: LTPs often contain targeting domains, motifs, transmembrane regions, amphipathic helices, or surface charges to define their donor and acceptor organelles.
source: LTPs often contain targeting domains, motifs, transmembrane regions, amphipathic helices, or surface charges to define their donor and acceptor organelles (Chiapparino et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chiapparino et al., 2016

claim: Many LTPs localize at two organelles simultaneously at membrane contact sites.
source: Many LTPs localize at two organelles simultaneously at membrane contact sites, where these organelles come closer to exchange information and material, including lipids (Scorrano et al., 2019; Prinz et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scorrano et al., 2019 and Prinz et al., 2020

claim: Membrane contact sites are locations where organelles come closer to exchange information and material, including lipids.
source: Many LTPs localize at two organelles simultaneously at membrane contact sites, where these organelles come closer to exchange information and material, including lipids (Scorrano et al., 2019; Prinz et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scorrano et al., 2019 and Prinz et al., 2020

claim: New LTPs and LTP families are being characterized regularly.
source: The human genome encodes over 150 LTPs; new LTPs and LTP families are being characterized every so often (Wong et al., 2019; Gatta et al., 2015; Sandhu et al., 2018; Valverde et al., 2019; Osawa et al., 2019; Yeo et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2018; Castro et al., 2022; Neuman et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations showing ongoing discovery

claim: LTPs feed metabolic lipid fluxes, eventually defining cellular lipid levels.
source: Since many lipid-modifying enzymes are localized to different organelles, LTPs also feed metabolic lipid fluxes, eventually defining cellular lipid levels (Holthuis and Menon, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holthuis and Menon, 2014

claim: Library-generated MelJuSo cells were grown in lipid-depleted serum for lipidomics analysis.
source: To this end, library-generated MelJuSo cells were grown in lipid-depleted serum and analyzed using a lipidomics platform detecting 17 different lipid classes thrice on average (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes the experimental methodology

claim: The lipidomics platform detected 17 different lipid classes.
source: To this end, library-generated MelJuSo cells were grown in lipid-depleted serum and analyzed using a lipidomics platform detecting 17 different lipid classes thrice on average (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes the experimental methodology

claim: Hexosylceramide can correspond to glucosylceramide and galactosylceramide, two isomeric lipids in mammalian cells.
source: One of the detected lipid classes, hexosylceramide, can correspond to glucosylceramide and galactosylceramide – two isomeric lipids in mammalian cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lipid chemistry

claim: Glucosylceramide is the major hexosylceramide in MelJuSo cells.
source: By metabolic chasing of a fluorescent ceramide analogue in cells silenced for glucosylceramide synthase or galactosylceramide synthase; or treated with the glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor PDMP, we validated that glucosylceramide is the major hexosylceramide in MelJuSo cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Validated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Galactosylceramide is present mainly in oligodendrocytes.
source: This further substantiated the previous reports of galactosylceramide being present mainly in oligodendrocytes (Reza et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reza et al., 2021

claim: No z-score above the absolute value of 2 was observed for NT control cells.
source: Meanwhile, no z-score above the absolute value of 2 was observed for NT control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: GLTP knockout cells showed lowered glucosylceramide levels.
source: In the analysis, we identified GLTP knockout cells with lowered glucosylceramide levels (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: Loss of GLTP blocks ER-to-Golgi anterograde vesicular trafficking that results in lowered glucosylceramide synthesis.
source: Loss of GLTP is recently reported to block ER-to-Golgi anterograde vesicular trafficking that results in lowered glucosylceramide synthesis (Nurmi et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nurmi et al., 2023

claim: NPC1 and NPC2 knockout cells have elevated sphingolipid levels.
source: In addition, we observed NPC1 and NPC2 knockout cells with elevated sphingolipid levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 1B

claim: Mutations in NPC1 and NPC2 genes cause Niemann-Pick disease, type C that leads to lysosomal accumulation of cholesterol.
source: Mutations in NPC1 and NPC2 genes are the cause of Niemann-Pick disease, type C that leads to lysosomal accumulation of cholesterol (Platt, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Platt, 2014

claim: Cells lacking NPC1 or NPC2 function accumulate sphingolipids.
source: Cells lacking NPC1 or NPC2 function also accumulate sphingolipids (Newton et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Newton et al., 2018

claim: The elevated sphingolipid levels in NPC1 and NPC2 knockout cells were present in all sphingolipid classes.
source: Our observation of elevated sphingolipid levels in NPC1 and NPC2 knockout cells was present in all sphingolipid classes (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: Phospholipid levels were not altered dramatically in NPC1 and NPC2 knockout cells.
source: Meanwhile, phospholipid levels were not altered dramatically in these cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Immunofluorescence staining of NPC1 and NPC2 knockout cells using a sphingomyelin biosensor showed lysosomal accumulation of sphingomyelin.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of NPC1 and NPC2 knockout cells using the biosensor showed lysosomal accumulation of sphingomyelin (Figure 2D).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 2D

claim: Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that sphingolipid accumulation is reflected on the cell surface of NPC1 and NPC2 knockouts.
source: Flow cytometry analysis using the sphingomyelin biosensor and the GM1 glycosphingolipid biosensor, the B subunit of cholera toxin, demonstrated that sphingolipid accumulation is also reflected on the cell surface of NPC1 and NPC2 knockouts (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: Surface protein levels were not altered in NPC1 and NPC2 knockouts as detected by staining for the tetraspanin protein CD63.
source: Meanwhile, the surface protein levels were not altered as detected by staining for the tetraspanin protein CD63.
evidence: Describes experimental results

claim: Sphingomyelin is the major sphingolipid in mammalian cells.
source: Sphingomyelin is the major sphingolipid in mammalian cells, and it is mainly synthesized in the trans-Golgi from ceramide delivered from the ER.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of sphingolipid metabolism

claim: Sphingomyelin is mainly synthesized in the trans-Golgi from ceramide delivered from the ER.
source: Sphingomyelin is the major sphingolipid in mammalian cells, and it is mainly synthesized in the trans-Golgi from ceramide delivered from the ER.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of sphingolipid metabolism

claim: The non-vesicular trafficking of ceramide from the ER to the trans-Golgi is mediated by the ceramide transfer protein CERT.
source: The non-vesicular trafficking of ceramide from the ER to the trans-Golgi is mediated by the ceramide transfer protein CERT (Hanada et al., 2003; Kumagai and Hanada, 2019; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanada et al., 2003 and Kumagai and Hanada, 2019

claim: CERT knockouts had the lowest sphingomyelin levels.
source: Our analysis identified CERT knockouts with the lowest sphingomyelin levels (Figures 1C and 3A).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figures 1C and 3A

claim: CERT knockout cells demonstrated increased glucosylceramide levels, likely as a compensation mechanism.
source: These cells also demonstrate increased glucosylceramide levels, likely as a compensation mechanism (Figure 3A).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 3A with speculative interpretation

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 knockout cells showed decreased sphingomyelin and increased glucosylceramide levels.
source: Furthermore, we found decreased sphingomyelin and increased glucosylceramide levels in ORP9 and ORP11 knockout cells – two proteins of unknown role in sphingolipid metabolism (Figures 1C and 3A).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figures 1C and 3A

claim: The sphingolipid imbalances in CERT, ORP9, and ORP11 knockout cells were represented in many sphingolipid subspecies.
source: The sphingolipid imbalances in all three knockout cells –CERT, ORP9, and ORP11– were also represented in many sphingolipid subspecies (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Lowered sphingomyelin levels of CERT, ORP9, and ORP11 knockout cells were confirmed by their sensitivity towards methyl-β-cyclodextrin treatment.
source: Lowered sphingomyelin levels of the three knockout cells were further confirmed by their sensitivity towards methyl-β-cyclodextrin treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 3D

claim: None of the CERT, ORP9, and ORP11 knockout cells demonstrated phospholipid imbalances to a compelling degree.
source: Meanwhile, none of the three knockout cells demonstrated phospholipid imbalances to a compelling degree (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Loss of ORP9 or ORP11 does not affect CERT protein levels.
source: The observation that ORP9 and ORP11 knockout cells mimic CERT knockouts implied a role for ORP9 and ORP11 in de novo sphingomyelin synthesis, whereas loss of neither ORP9 nor ORP11 reduced CERT protein levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 3E

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 each contain a PH domain mediating localization at the trans-Golgi.
source: ORP9 and ORP11 each contain a PH domain mediating localization at the trans-Golgi, the site of de novo sphingomyelin synthesis (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Describes protein domain architecture shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: Loss of either ORP9 or ORP11 did not alter the Golgi ultrastructure as detected by light or electron microscopy.
source: As loss of either ORP9 or ORP11 did not alter the Golgi ultrastructure as detected by light or electron microscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), it further suggested that ORP9 and ORP11 affect sphingomyelin levels by a previously unknown mechanism.
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 interact with each other via their regions between their PH and ORD domains.
source: ORP9 and ORP11 interact with each other via their regions between their PH and ORD domains (Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2010

claim: AlphaFold and PCOILS coiled coils prediction tool suggested that ORP9 and ORP11 contain two alpha helices each in the region between their PH and ORD domains.
source: AlphaFold and PCOILS coiled coils prediction tool suggested that ORP9 and ORP11 contain two alpha helices each in this region – hereafter referred to as 'coils' (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Based on computational predictions shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: AlphaFold-Multimer suggested that the coils of ORP9 and ORP11 interact with each other.
source: AlphaFold-Multimer suggested that the coils of ORP9 and ORP11 interact with each other (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Based on computational predictions shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D

claim: Analysis of the full-length proteins predicted that the coils drive the dimerization of ORP9 and ORP11.
source: Identical analysis of the full-length proteins predicted that the coils drive the dimerization of the two proteins (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on computational predictions shown in Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: In cells expressing mitochondria-targeted ORP9 coils, the coils of ORP11 are located in mitochondria.
source: This was tested by targeting the coils of ORP9 to the mitochondrial outer membrane using the N-terminal sequence of TOM70. In cells expressing mitochondria-targeted ORP9 coils, the coils of ORP11 are located in this organelle (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: The absence of either coil prevented the colocalization of ORP9 and ORP11 coils at mitochondria.
source: The absence of either coil prevented the colocalization, suggesting that the coils of ORP9 and ORP11 are sufficient for their dimerization.
evidence: Describes experimental results

claim: The coils of ORP9 and ORP11 are sufficient for their dimerization.
source: The absence of either coil prevented the colocalization, suggesting that the coils of ORP9 and ORP11 are sufficient for their dimerization.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: The dimerization of ORP9 and ORP11 via their coils was validated by co-immunoprecipitations.
source: This finding was validated by co-immunoprecipitations (Figure 4E).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 4E

claim: ORP9 contains a FFAT motif that drives ER localization by interacting with the ER-resident VAPA and VAPB.
source: ORP9, but not ORP11, contains a FFAT, two phenylalanines in an acidic tract, a motif that drives ER localization by interacting with the ER-resident VAPA and VAPB (Neefjes and Cabukusta, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neefjes and Cabukusta, 2021

claim: ORP11 does not contain a FFAT motif.
source: ORP9, but not ORP11, contains a FFAT, two phenylalanines in an acidic tract, a motif that drives ER localization by interacting with the ER-resident VAPA and VAPB (Neefjes and Cabukusta, 2021).
evidence: Describes protein domain architecture

claim: ORP11 can interact with VAPA and VAPB by its dimerization with ORP9.
source: Despite not containing a FFAT motif, ORP11 could interact with VAPA and VAPB by its dimerization with ORP9.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: ORP11 could be co-isolated with VAPA from cells expressing VAPA, ORP9, and ORP11.
source: We tested this by co-immunoprecipitations, where ORP11 could be co-isolated with VAPA from cells expressing VAPA, ORP9, and ORP11 (Figure 4J).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 4J

claim: The interaction between ORP11 and VAPA was diminished significantly when ORP9 was not co-expressed.
source: This interaction was diminished significantly when ORP9 was not co-expressed.
evidence: Describes experimental results

claim: A VAPA mutant unable to interact with FFAT motifs failed to interact with either ORP9 or ORP11.
source: Furthermore, a VAPA mutant unable to interact with FFAT motifs failed to interact with either ORP9 or ORP11, showing that ORP11 interacts with VAPA indirectly via the ORP9-FFAT motif.
evidence: Describes experimental results

claim: ORP11 interacts with VAPA indirectly via the ORP9-FFAT motif.
source: Furthermore, a VAPA mutant unable to interact with FFAT motifs failed to interact with either ORP9 or ORP11, showing that ORP11 interacts with VAPA indirectly via the ORP9-FFAT motif.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: The human proteome contains three other proteins interacting with FFAT and related short linear motifs: MOSPD1, MOSPD2, and MOSPD3.
source: We and others previously showed that in addition to VAPA and VAPB, the human proteome contains three other proteins interacting with FFAT and related short linear motifs: MOSPD1, MOSPD2, and MOSPD3 (Di Mattia et al., 2018; Cabukusta et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Mattia et al., 2018 and Cabukusta et al., 2020

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 were found in proximity with VAPA and VAPB but not with other motif-binding proteins in BioID analysis.
source: In this analysis, ORP9 and ORP11 were found in proximity with VAPA and VAPB but not with other motif-binding proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Describes results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F

claim: The Golgi localization of ORP9 and ORP11 is mediated by their PH domain interacting with phosphatidylinositol phosphates.
source: The Golgi localization of ORP9 and ORP11 is mediated by their PH domain interacting with phosphatidylinositol phosphates (Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2010

claim: The PH domains of ORP9 and ORP11 localized only partially to the Golgi and demonstrated strong cytoplasmic localization.
source: We observed that the PH domains of ORP9 and ORP11 localized only partially to the Golgi and demonstrated strong cytoplasmic localization, unlike the PH domains of OSBP and CERT that show exclusive localization to this organelle (Levine and Munro, 1998; Levine and Munro, 2002; Figure 4H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 4H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I

claim: The PH domains of OSBP and CERT show exclusive localization to the Golgi.
source: We observed that the PH domains of ORP9 and ORP11 localized only partially to the Golgi and demonstrated strong cytoplasmic localization, unlike the PH domains of OSBP and CERT that show exclusive localization to this organelle (Levine and Munro, 1998; Levine and Munro, 2002; Figure 4H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levine and Munro, 1998 and Levine and Munro, 2002

claim: A chimera containing ORP9- and ORP11-PH domains localized to the Golgi more efficiently than the individual PH domains.
source: To test this, we created a chimera containing ORP9- and ORP11-PH domains that localized to the Golgi more efficiently than the individual PH domains (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 4H,I

claim: The dimerization of ORP9 and ORP11 is a mechanism to increase their avidity towards trans-Golgi membranes.
source: We hypothesized that the dimerization of ORP9 and ORP11 is a mechanism to increase their avidity towards trans-Golgi membranes.
evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental observations

claim: Loss of either ORP9 or ORP11 reduces the other's localization to the trans-Golgi.
source: This also implied that loss of either protein should reduce the other's localization to the trans-Golgi. Immunofluorescence staining of ORP9 and ORP11 knockout cells for the same proteins confirmed that both ORP9 and ORP11 are required for the Golgi localization of the other protein (Figure 5).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 5

claim: Loss of either ORP9 or ORP11 did not influence the levels of the other protein.
source: Meanwhile, loss of either protein did not influence the levels of the other (Figure 3E).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 3E

claim: The dimerization of ORP9 and ORP11 via their coils is required for the localization of ORP9-ORP11 dimer to the ER and the trans-Golgi simultaneously.
source: Our results collectively show that the dimerization of ORP9 and ORP11 via their coils is required for the localization of ORP9-ORP11 dimer to the ER and the trans-Golgi simultaneously.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 belong to the OSBP-related protein (ORP) family that transfers sterols or PS while transferring phosphatidylinositol phosphates in the opposite direction.
source: ORP9 and ORP11 belong to the OSBP-related protein (ORP) family that transfers sterols or PS while transferring phosphatidylinositol phosphates in the opposite direction (Wang et al., 2019; Mesmin et al., 2013; de Saint-Jean et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 2013; Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 carry the conserved PS binding site.
source: ORP9 and ORP11 carry the conserved PS binding site and are recently shown to relocate to the site of lysosomal damage to supply PS for membrane repair (Tan and Finkel, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tan and Finkel, 2022

claim: ORP9 and ORP11 are recently shown to relocate to the site of lysosomal damage to supply PS for membrane repair.
source: ORP9 and ORP11 carry the conserved PS binding site and are recently shown to relocate to the site of lysosomal damage to supply PS for membrane repair (Tan and Finkel, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tan and Finkel, 2022

claim: The lipid transfer domains (ORD) of ORP9 and ORP11 are sufficient to traffic PS in vitro.
source: Using an in vitro lipid transfer assay, we confirmed that the lipid transfer domains (ORD) of ORP9 and ORP11 are sufficient to traffic PS in vitro (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: ORP9 and ORP10 are shown to traffic PI(4)P.
source: ORP9 and ORP10, but not ORP11, are shown to traffic PI(4)P (Kawasaki et al., 2022; He et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kawasaki et al., 2022 and He et al., 2023

claim: ORD of ORP11 can traffic PI(4)P between model membranes.
source: Using a PI(4)P transfer assay that utilizes the PI(4)P-binding PH domain of FAPP1, we show that ORD of ORP11 can also traffic PI(4)P between model membranes (Figure 6D and E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D; Ikhlef et al., 2021).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 6D and E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: The PS-trafficking activity of ORP9- and ORP11-ORDs was improved when acceptor liposomes were decorated with PI(4)P.
source: Furthermore, similar to ORP5, ORP8, and ORP10, the PS-trafficking activity of ORP9- and ORP11-ORDs was improved when acceptor liposomes were decorated with PI(4)P (Kawasaki et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2015; Moser von Filseck et al., 2015; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: ORDs of ORP9 and ORP11 transport PI(4)P in the opposite direction of PS trafficking.
source: This indicated that ORDs of ORP9 and ORP11 transport PI(4)P in the opposite direction of PS trafficking.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: The ORP9-ORP11-VAPB complex displays an improved lipid transfer capacity as a trimer in reconstituted contact sites.
source: PS transfer assay in these reconstituted contact sites showed that as a trimer, the ORP9-ORP11-VAPB complex displays an improved lipid transfer capacity (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: Describes experimental results shown in Figure 6G and H

claim: PS is synthesized in the ER and its concentration increases along the secretory pathway as it is enriched on the cytosolic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: PS is synthesized in the ER and its concentration increases along the secretory pathway as it is enriched on the cytosolic leaflet of the plasma membrane (Holthuis and Menon, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holthuis and Menon, 2014

claim: PI(4)P is abundant in the trans-Golgi, where it recruits many proteins to this membrane.
source: PI(4)P, on the other hand, is abundant in the trans-Golgi, where it recruits many proteins to this membrane (Posor et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Posor et al., 2022

claim: OSBP transfers cholesterol from the ER to the trans-Golgi, while counter-transporting PI(4)P to the ER for its hydrolysis by the ER-resident PI(4)P phosphatase SAC1.
source: Another LTP localized at the ER-trans Golgi membrane contact sites, OSBP transfers cholesterol from the ER to the trans-Golgi, while counter-transporting PI(4)P to the ER for its hydrolysis by the ER-resident PI(4)P phosphatase SAC1 (Figure 8).
evidence: Based on established knowledge shown in Figure 8

claim: PS levels were decreased in the Golgi of ORP9 and ORP11 knockout cells.
source: Golgi localization of these sensors indicated that PS levels were decreased in the Golgi of these cells (Figure 6I and J).
